value.name: Experiment 1a: a cloze diagnostic for telicity (contentful condition)
value.description: Participants completed each event description with three in-line dropdowns (preposition in/for; numeral; time unit), choosing the values they found most natural (paper §2). Generality was manipulated between participants; this record is the contentful condition.
labels: in
for
value.guidelines:
In this study, we are interested in how long things tend to take. To investigate this question, we will give you sentences with blanks in them and ask you to fill in those blanks with the values that you think are most natural using the dropdowns we provide.

For example, you might receive the following sentence:

The child ate the sandwich .

A natural way to complete this sentence might be in 5 minutes, which you would indicate by selecting in from the first dropdown, 5 from the second, and minutes from the third.

Alternatively, you might consider in 30 seconds or in 1 hour more natural, depending on how long you think it generally takes children to eat sandwiches. In cases like this, where multiple options are natural, choose the one you think is most natural.

This research is being carried out by Dr. Aaron White at the University of Rochester. You can read more about the study here. Upon clicking continue, you will enter fullscreen mode.

value.name: Experiment 1b: a temporal-overlap diagnostic for durativity (contentful condition)
value.description: Each event description was shown with a fixed temporal modifier (in/for + numeral + time unit), followed by the question 'For what proportion of those N units (if any) was [the event happening]?' and five ordered options (paper §3). The response is coded 0 (none) to 4 (the entirety). This record is the contentful condition.
labels: None of those N units
Less than half of those N units
About half of those N units
More than half of those N units
The entirety of those N units
value.guidelines:
In this study, we are interested in how long things tend to take. To investigate this question, we will give you a sentence describing something that happened, along with some amount of time, and we will ask you what proportion of that time (if any) that thing took up.

For example, you might receive the following sentence and question:

A natural response might be more than half of those 5 minutes. Alternatively, you might think that eating a sandwich would take up all of those five minutes, in which case you would respond the entirety of those 5 minutes, or you might think that eating a sandwich would take up only about half of those 5 minutes. Multiple answers may make sense, and you should click the response you think is most likely.

In certain cases, the thing that happened may not take any of the time mentioned in the sentence. For example, you might receive the following sentence and question:

In this case, we know that the arrival didn't take any of the 20 minutes mentioned because it happened only after those 20 minutes had elapsed, so you would answer none of those 20 minutes. Answering less than half of those 20 minutes would also be correct, but if you can answer none of those 20 minutes, as you can here, you should.

This research is being carried out by Dr. Aaron White at the University of Rochester. You can read more about the study here. Upon clicking continue, you will enter fullscreen mode.

value.name: Experiment 2: sense similarity
value.description: Each trial paired two event descriptions sharing a verb, without temporal modifiers; participants rated how different the described situations are on a continuous slider from 'completely identical' (0, left) to 'extremely different' (100, right). Each participant first rated eight calibration pairs from Cao et al. (2024), excluded from analysis (§5).
labels: completely identical
extremely different
value.guidelines:
In this study, we are interested in how different situations are from each other. To investigate this question, we will give you two sentences describing situations, and we will ask you to judge how different those situations are using a slider.

For example, you might receive the following two sentences:

The athlete ran the marathon.

The CEO ran the company.

completely identical
extremely different

A natural response might be that the situations described by these two sentences are very different, and so you would slide the slider pretty far to the right.

You might also receive the following two sentences:

The teenager ran the 800m.

The highschooler ran the race.

completely identical
extremely different

In this case, you might judge these as nearly identical (if not completely identical), so you would slide the slider pretty far to the left.

The slider will always start at completely identical on the left, and you will need to move the slider in order to submit your response. If you judge the two situations to be completely identical, you can simply click on the slider and response submission will become available.

This research is being carried out by Dr. Aaron White at the University of Rochester. You can read more about the study here. Upon clicking continue, you will enter fullscreen mode.
